language_wrapper: Consider an {rows} by {cols} grid. Each cell is colored black, gray, or white under the rules: (i) no two black cells are orthogonally adjacent; (ii) no two gray cells are diagonally adjacent; (iii) no black cell is orthogonally adjacent to any gray cell. Let N(r, c, k, t) be the number of such colorings with exactly k black cells and exactly t gray cells. Compute N({rows}, {cols}, {k_black}, {t_gray}).
hardness_rationale: The family generalizes the seed by moving from two colors (black/white) and orthogonal-adjacency avoidance to three colors with coupled constraints: black cells avoid both black and gray orthogonally, while gray cells avoid gray diagonally. The problem additionally fixes the exact counts of black and gray cells, requiring a bivariate transfer-matrix dynamic program over row states and a compatibility graph, rather than a single-parameter recurrence. This significantly increases state-space size, introduces multi-type interactions across rows, and demands careful counting of coefficients, making guessing infeasible and the solution method more advanced.
notes: Proof of correctness (outline): Model each row as a state over {W,G,B} that satisfies intra-row constraints (no B adjacent to B or G). Construct a compatibility graph between consecutive rows: orth adjacency forbids B above anything non-W and forbids G above B; diagonal adjacency forbids G diagonals. The total number of colorings with exactly k black and t gray cells equals the sum over all length-r paths in this graph of the product of 1's (each state occurrence contributes counts b_s and g_s). This is captured by a dynamic program that accumulates the joint counts (k, t) across rows using transfer along compatible edges. The DP computes the exact coefficient of x^k y^t in the bivariate generating function defined by the transfer matrix, establishing correctness. Implementation notes: we restrict rows, cols ∈ [4,7] so that 3^cols and DP remain tractable; the generator filters for instances with sufficiently large counts to ensure nontrivial difficulty.
source_question: The number of ways to color an \(n \times n\) chessboard with black and white such that no neighboring two blocks can be black simultaneously is \(x_n\). Find \(\sum_{n=2}^5 x_n\)．
